Turn any outfit reference into a professional fashion character sheet. ✨👗
Just upload your outfit image and let AI handle the rest.
Created with @ChatGPT 
Prompt :
Create a premium professional fashion design character sheet based strictly on the provided reference image of the clothing/outfit.

The uploaded reference image is the primary and authoritative source for the outfit design. Analyze it carefully and reconstruct the clothing as accurately as possible while preserving its original design identity, silhouette, proportions, materials, colors, patterns, construction, accessories, and distinctive details.

The final result must look like a high-end professional fashion design / costume development presentation board, similar to a luxury fashion brand's internal design specification sheet.

1. OUTFIT REFERENCE LOCK

Use the uploaded clothing reference as the design source of truth.

Preserve:

exact garment type and overall silhouette
original colors and color relationships
fabric appearance
prints, patterns, stripes, checks, embroidery and graphics
collars, necklines and lapels
sleeves, cuffs and hems
buttons, zippers, buckles and closures
pockets and seams
stitching and construction details
layering structure
straps, belts and hardware
footwear
bags and other visible accessories
distinctive design elements

Do not redesign, simplify, modernize, beautify, or replace the outfit.

If the reference contains multiple clothing pieces, identify and reproduce every visible component separately.

If something is partially hidden in the reference, intelligently reconstruct it while remaining consistent with the visible design.

2. PROFESSIONAL CHARACTER SHEET PRESENTATION

Create a vertical 4:5 professional fashion presentation board with a clean editorial layout.

Place the complete outfit prominently in the center, presented as a professional fashion product/design visualization.

The clothing should be clearly visible from top to bottom.

Use a clean isolated presentation style, preferably on a sophisticated warm-white / ivory / very light neutral background.

The composition should resemble:

Luxury Fashion Lookbook + Costume Design Sheet + Technical Outfit Specification Board

Do NOT make it look like a normal fashion photograph.

Do NOT place the outfit on a distracting model unless the reference specifically requires a model-based presentation.

Prefer a clean floating garment / invisible mannequin / professionally arranged outfit presentation so the clothing itself remains the primary focus.

3. DESIGN BREAKDOWN

Surround the main outfit with professional annotation callouts.

Add thin elegant leader lines pointing toward important garment details.

Create approximately 6–10 numbered detail callouts, depending on how many meaningful elements exist in the reference.

Examples:

01 — Main Garment
Identify the primary clothing piece and its construction.

02 — Upper Detail
Describe collar, neckline, lapel, shoulder or upper construction.

03 — Sleeve / Cuff Detail
Describe sleeve shape, cuff construction, buttons or finishing.

04 — Fabric & Texture
Describe visible material, weave, finish, texture or surface quality.

05 — Pattern / Print Detail
Describe checks, stripes, graphics, embroidery, motifs or decorative elements.

06 — Closure / Hardware
Describe buttons, zipper, buckle, snaps, chains or other hardware.

07 — Lower Garment
Describe trousers, skirt, shorts, dress structure or other lower-body component.

08 — Accessories / Footwear
Describe shoes, bag, belt, jewelry or other visible accessories.

Only include categories that are actually relevant to the reference.

4. MATERIAL & DETAIL PANEL

Add a dedicated MATERIAL & DETAIL section.

Show several small professional close-up crops of the outfit focusing on:

fabric texture
stitching
embroidery
buttons
hardware
prints
seams
trims
distinctive construction details

Each crop should look like a professional fashion-development reference photograph.

Use small numbered labels beneath the details.

5. COLOR PALETTE

Add a COLOR PALETTE section.

Extract the dominant colors directly from the reference outfit.

Display approximately 4–7 clean circular color swatches.

Under each swatch, provide a short professional color name such as:

Ivory
Charcoal
Burgundy
Olive
Navy
Sand
Black

Do not invent unrelated colors.

The palette must accurately represent the actual clothing.

6. COORDINATE / DESIGN NOTES

Add a small professional text section titled:

COORDINATE NOTE

Briefly explain:

overall styling direction
silhouette
layering
visual balance
relationship between garments
distinctive design language

Keep the text concise and editorial.

7. APPEAL POINT

Add a section titled:

APPEAL POINT

List approximately 4–6 short design highlights explaining what makes the outfit visually distinctive.

Examples may include:

distinctive silhouette
contrast detailing
structured tailoring
layered construction
statement hardware
unique pattern placement
unusual proportions
refined finishing

These observations must be based on the actual reference.

8. STYLING LOGIC

Add a small section titled:

STYLING LOGIC

Explain how the individual pieces work together visually and why the combination creates the overall look.

Keep it concise, professional and fashion-editorial.

9. TYPOGRAPHY & GRAPHIC DESIGN

Use a premium minimalist fashion-editorial typography system.

Use:

elegant serif typography for major headings
clean modern sans-serif for technical information
thin fine-line dividers
subtle numbered labels
precise leader lines
balanced margins
generous negative space
sophisticated editorial hierarchy

The page should feel like a real luxury fashion house design document, not an AI-generated poster.

Do not overcrowd the page.

10. IMAGE QUALITY & REALISM

Ultra-realistic professional fashion photography / product visualization.

Extremely high detail.

Accurate fabric behavior.

Realistic stitching.

Realistic material texture.

Physically believable garment construction.

Sharp garment edges.

Natural shadows.

Subtle studio lighting.

Premium commercial photography quality.

Clean high-resolution rendering.

No artificial plastic appearance.

No CGI-looking surfaces.

No distorted garments.

No random accessories.

No unnecessary decorative elements.

11. UNIVERSAL OUTFIT ADAPTATION

This prompt must work regardless of the uploaded outfit.

The reference may contain:

men's clothing
women's clothing
children's clothing
unisex clothing
casualwear
formalwear
streetwear
sportswear
uniforms
traditional clothing
cultural clothing
bridalwear
eveningwear
fantasy costumes
historical clothing
futuristic clothing
outerwear
complete outfits
single garments
garments with accessories

Automatically adapt the character sheet structure to whatever is actually present in the reference image.

Do not force irrelevant sections or clothing categories.

If the reference contains only one garment, focus the sheet on that garment.

If it contains a complete outfit, document the complete outfit.

If accessories are present, include them.

If accessories are absent, do not invent them.

12. ABSOLUTE ACCURACY RULE

REFERENCE IMAGE > CREATIVE INTERPRETATION

The uploaded reference always takes priority.

Do not change:

garment identity
silhouette
color
pattern
proportions
construction
distinctive details

unless necessary to reconstruct an obscured portion that is not visible.

The final character sheet should make it possible for a fashion designer, costume designer, illustrator, or AI image-generation system to understand exactly what the original outfit looks like and how it is constructed.

FINAL OUTPUT

A single polished 4:5 vertical professional fashion character sheet, centered around the accurately reconstructed reference outfit, with elegant editorial layout, technical callouts, material/detail crops, color palette, styling notes, and professional fashion-design documentation.

Premium fashion house aesthetic.
Minimal. Sophisticated. Technical. Editorial. Ultra-realistic.
No unnecessary creativity. Preserve the reference design.

Prompt:
[Generation Goal]

Generate a continuous high-end cinematic sports fashion commercial video featuring the same model Rinko-Pink ( @). Keep her face, hairstyle, white baseball cap, white sports jacket, loose white shorts and white sneakers completely consistent. Background geometric graphics continuously animate and transform while the model poses naturally like a professional fashion shoot and the camera switches freely between angles.

[Reference Asset Roles]

@ is used for the opening extreme close-up pose, facial features, white Nike cap, white jacket with black stripes, and the large pink circle background composition.

@ is used for the low-angle full-body crouching pose, complete outfit including white shorts, white Nike socks and chunky white sneakers, and the pink/black geometric studio set.

@ is used for the profile close-up, upward gaze, hair silhouette against the pink-and-black striped background.

@ is used for the wink close-up expression, slightly lower camera angle, and hair partially covering the face.

@ is used for the low-angle beauty close-up, soft chin lift, and facial lighting.

@ jointly define the single model Rinko-Pink: face from all angles (front, three-quarter, side), eye and lip details, full body front/side/back views of the white Nike tracksuit, shorts, socks and sneakers, and exact cap/shoe details. They establish the fixed identity, proportions and clothing throughout.

[Subjects and Relationships]

Rinko-Pink ( @ ) is the sole character. She always retains the exact face, long dark hair with bangs, white Nike baseball cap, white oversized windbreaker with black side stripes, white crop top, loose white shorts, white Nike crew socks and white chunky Nike sneakers. No other people appear. Background is a clean white studio with continuously transforming pink, black and white geometric vector shapes.

[Event Script]

Shot 1 @— Extreme Close-up

Video opens on the extreme facial close-up of Rinko-Pink. She stares directly into the lens, then slowly extends her right hand toward the camera so the hand enters the foreground with natural shallow-depth-of-field blur. She tilts her head slightly; hair and bangs drift softly with air movement. The huge pink circle and white arcs in the background slowly slide horizontally and morph. Camera performs a gentle dolly-in.

Shot 2 @— Low Angle Full Body

Hard cut to a low-angle wide full-body shot. Rinko-Pink crouches on the white studio floor, one knee raised, elbow resting on the knee while supporting her chin. She then naturally adjusts her posture and looks toward the camera. Camera slowly tracks sideways from the low position. Black-and-white vertical stripes shift left-right while pink rectangles slide in from the walls and rearrange themselves.

Shot 3 @— Profile Close-up

Quick cut to a clean profile close-up. Rinko-Pink tilts her head slightly upward, eyes looking up, then slowly turns her gaze toward the lens. The white cap brim and long hair create a sharp silhouette. The large pink circle in the background gradually becomes a semicircle and arcs; black geometric frames slowly rotate, producing flat graphic-animation motion.

Shot 4 @— Wink Close-up

Cut to a slightly lower close-up. Rinko-Pink gently closes one eye in a soft wink, then returns to a normal gaze. The cap brim partially shades her forehead; hair sways lightly with the motion. Pink and black geometric shapes slowly rotate, scale and recompose behind her.

Shot 5 @ — Low-angle Beauty Close-up

Camera shoots from a slightly low angle. Rinko-Pink lifts her chin gently, looks down toward the lens, then lightly adjusts the cap brim with her fingers. Camera performs a slow push-in into an ultra-close beauty shot of her eyes and face. Pink arcs, black rectangles and white space continue moving, finally settling into a clean pink geometric composition.

Overall motion and style:

Dynamic geometric background animation with continuous vector-shape transformations (slides, flips, enlarge, morph, shrink, wipe, zoom, spins, bounce) that transition smoothly from shot to shot. Pastel pink and white color palette with black geometric accents. Fashion-editorial photography, spontaneous natural model posing, multiple camera angles (extreme close-up, profile, low-angle, wide), dolly-in, tracking, smooth camera transitions. Realistic human movement, natural hair physics, realistic clothing fabric movement. Soft high-key studio lighting, shallow depth of field, photorealistic, premium sports fashion commercial, clean minimalist studio, sophisticated composition, low contrast, natural skin texture. No dialogue, no subtitles.

[Maintain Consistency]

Keep Rinko-Pink’s face, hairstyle, white Nike cap, white jacket with black stripes, loose white shorts, white socks and white sneakers identical across every shot. Maintain exact clothing ownership, body proportions and studio spatial relationships. Background remains pure geometric animation without people or props.

Generative language modeling for antibody CDR grafting and alignment-driven de novo design

1. The paper introduces GenCDR, a framework-first autoregressive (LLaMA-style) antibody language model: it reads all framework regions (FR1–FR4) as the prompt, then generates all CDRs jointly as a variable-length response, creating a clean prompt–response boundary for reward attribution and alignment.

2. This re-ordering directly targets the core de novo antibody problem as an infilling task: CDR design conditioned on a fixed scaffold. Unlike left-to-right decoding (where early CDRs lack downstream framework context), GenCDR generates CDRs with full framework context available from the start.

3. GenCDR is presented as a model family covering common design settings: IgGenCDR (unpaired human OAS, ~254M sequences), p-IgGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~1.8M natively paired VH–VL sequences), and NanoGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~6.5M camelid VHH from INDI plus human OAS heavy chains in a 1:1 mixture to preserve humanness on humanized scaffolds).

4. On CDR recovery (next-token prediction accuracy over CDR tokens) using a CDR3-disjoint held-out test set designed to reduce leakage, framework-first ordering improves over a same-sized left-to-right ablation and surpasses prior autoregressive baselines (including p-IgGen, ProGen2-OAS, and IgLM) across essentially all loops, with especially strong gains where downstream context matters most (e.g., CDR1).

5. De novo generation quality: when prompted with held-out frameworks and sampling CDRs jointly, GenCDR reproduces natural CDR length distributions closely (across all loops), while maintaining human-likeness (OASis), naturalness (ESM-2 PLL), and diversity/novelty with smooth trade-offs across sampling temperatures.

6. A key design consequence of the framework-first factorization is separable CDR likelihoods: GenCDR can score only the generated CDR block (rather than conflating framework+CDR likelihood), enabling clearer optimization targets and more principled alignment for CDR-centric objectives.

7. Likelihoods retain useful biological signal: GenCDR log-likelihood correlates zero-shot with experimental fitness/developability benchmarks (FLAb). The analysis also highlights assay locality: immunogenicity appears more CDR-driven, while expression is more framework-driven, and paired scoring (p-IgGenCDR) improves correlations when heavy+light are scored jointly.

8. NanoGenCDR extends the framework-first approach to nanobodies: fine-tuning closes the human→camelid distribution shift in CDR recovery, generates plausible/developable VHHs (including fold-confidence and developability flag rates comparable to reference), and improves humanness on humanized VHH scaffolds specifically due to the camelid+human mixture strategy.

9. Alignment-driven de novo design: the prompt–response boundary enables iterative alignment with weighted DPO (wDPO) using rewards computed only on the generated CDR completion. They optimize a composite reward from antibody–antigen co-folding metrics (Boltz-2) plus non-differentiable developability liability rules, demonstrating multi-objective steering without explicit antigen encoding in the model input.

10. In a PD-L1 nanobody design benchmark, four rounds of alignment drive near-perfect compliance with length/liability constraints after one round (acceptance ~23.8% → ~99.8–100%), and achieve in silico interface metrics competitive with a structure-conditioned diffusion pipeline (BoltzGen) at roughly half the sampling budget, while producing sequences that remain more “natural” under independent language-model scoring—suggesting KL-anchored alignment can push target-facing metrics without excessive distributional drift.

What is PPO vs DPO vs GRPO? (in AI engineer interviews)

Let's learn together ↓

These are three different recipes for aligning LLMs with human preferences.

They all try to make a model produce better outputs. But they disagree on how to measure "better" and what machinery you need to get there.

The tradeoff is always the same: more control vs. less memory vs. fewer assumptions.

The formulas:

PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization):
L_CLIP = E[ min(r_t × A_t, clip(r_t, 1-ε, 1+ε) × A_t) ]

Where:
r_t → ratio of new policy to old policy (π_θ / π_old)
A_t → advantage estimate from value network
ε → clipping range, keeps updates inside a trust region

DPO (Direct Preference Optimization):
L_DPO = -log σ(β log π_θ(y_w)/π_ref(y_w) - β log π_θ(y_l)/π_ref(y_l))

Where:
y_w → the preferred (winning) response
y_l → the rejected (losing) response
β → controls how sharp the gradient signal is
π_ref → frozen reference policy (SFT model)

GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization):
Â_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r), where r = {r_1, ..., r_G}

Where:
r_i → reward for the i-th output in the group
G → number of sampled outputs per prompt
Â_i → z-scored advantage, replaces the value network

How each one works:

PPO:
1. Sample a response from the current policy
2. Score it with a learned reward model, subtract KL penalty
3. Estimate advantages using a value network (GAE)
4. Update policy with clipped objective, stay near old policy

DPO:
1. Collect static preference pairs (prompt, y_w, y_l)
2. Keep a frozen reference policy
3. Compute log-ratio differences for both responses
4. Minimize the log-sigmoid loss directly, no reward model needed

GRPO:
1. For each prompt, sample G outputs from the policy
2. Score each with a reward model
3. Z-score the rewards across the group to get advantages
4. Run a PPO-style update, no value network required

🧐 How do they actually differ?

Memory cost:
PPO needs 4 models (policy, ref, reward, value). DPO needs 2 (policy, ref). GRPO sits in between at 2-3.

Data requirement:
PPO and GRPO need online rollouts. DPO works offline with pre-collected pairs, no sampling budget needed.

Reward type:
PPO uses a learned reward model. DPO bakes the reward signal into the loss implicitly. GRPO expects verifiable rewards (math answers, code tests, format checks).

Baseline:
PPO uses a value network to reduce variance. GRPO replaces that with group z-scoring. DPO skips the baseline problem entirely.

When to use each:
PPO when you have a dense reward signal and token-level credit assignment matters. DPO when you have static preference pairs and no online sampling budget. GRPO when rewards are verifiable (math, code, format) and running many rollouts per prompt is cheap.

The partnership will allow invited guests to see themselves in the new collection as it debuts, offering a more personal and interactive way to experience fashion week. Alice + Olivia’s show takes place at 583 Park Avenue on Thursday.

The activation of Glance’s AI-powered virtual try-on technology gives Alice + Olivia a new way to engage guests as AI moves fashion discovery beyond static look books and product grids toward experiences built around the individual shopper. Glance serves as the official AI and technology partner for Alice + Olivia during NYFW. At the presentation, attendees can visit the Glance experience to generate images of themselves wearing selected pieces from the spring 2027 collection.

Glance, an intelligent shopping agent, is powered by proprietary agentic intelligence and generative AI. It delivers a hyper-personalized consumer experience across mobile and TV. - Bilevel Coordinated Reflection: a game-theoretic look at multi-agent LLM coordination and memory

either Instagram is pushing ai content too much, or the agentic content pipeline I created is really good.

I was bored and didn’t know what to do with so many gemini credits, so I built an agentic creative studio which handles script, storyboard, keyframes, shot generation, music, captions, editing, and delivers the final video to me after I tell it a topic to build on.

I tested this on a fresh Instagram account (no warmup) and got around 1.1 million+ views in about 3 weeks.

the format of the videos is LEGO style storytelling of Indian mythology, and the same workflow could be extended to AI influencers creating UGC on fashion, skincare, GRWM, in fact anything.

I will try it on a few more fresh accounts. let’s see how it goes.
